transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Thank you so much for seeing me, it's very nice to meet you too. 

Um... well, I hope it's okay that I'm here. I guess what finally brought me in is... I've just been feeling a little, I don't know, a little flat lately? Not terrible, really! Just... it feels like the part of me that used to really reach for people, or take joy in my work, has gone very quiet. 

I used to love my yoga classes, and going to art galleries, and even just journaling in the evenings. But lately, I'm mostly just... moving through obligations, I suppose. I'm still getting everything done, of course! I'm a social worker, so I know I have to keep showing up for my clients. But... does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it right. I just didn't want to let it go on too long without checking in with someone.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Um, let's see... I think it's been about eight months? Yes, roughly eight months. That's when we took my older relative into our apartment to live with us. 

Which is a good thing, really! I'm so glad we can be there for them, and I really don't mind helping out. But... I suppose that's when I started noticing this whole change in how I'm thinking, and working, and connecting with people. I guess it’s just been a bit of an adjustment, sharing the space and everything. 

I hope it doesn't sound terrible of me to say that having family move in might have thrown me off a little bit. I'd hate to sound selfish. Is it normal for a change at home to make you feel this way?
Aside from feeling flat, have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns since this started?

Oh, my sleep? Um... no, I don't think so. I've been sleeping just fine, really! I mean, I try to make sure I get a good night's rest so I can be present for my clients and, you know, for my relative at home. 

I haven't noticed any major changes, honestly. Maybe just the normal amount of being a little tired after a long day? But nothing unusual, I promise. I hope that's an okay answer? I just haven't really had any trouble in that department.
Have you experienced these feelings of being 'flat' or losing interest in your usual activities at any point in your life before this relative moved in eight months ago?

Um, before eight months ago? No, I really don't think so. I've always been a pretty upbeat person, you know? I mean, I love my job and I've always tried to be really engaged with life. 

I've never really felt this... disconnected before. I've always been the one organizing outings or getting excited about new projects at work. So this is all very new to me. I hope I'm not making a bigger deal out of it than I should be! I know everyone has their off days, or even off months. Does that sound like a normal way to feel, having this happen for the first time now?
Do you feel that this 'flat' feeling has caused you any significant distress, or is it making it harder for you to perform your daily tasks at work or at home?

Um, well... I'm still managing to show up for work every day, I promise! I really try to be there for my team. But, um... I guess it has been a little harder than usual to keep up with everything. 

I feel terrible admitting this, but... I've actually missed a couple of grant deadlines recently. And, well, my supervisor—she's so wonderful and understanding—she’s quietly moved some of my more demanding clients to other clinicians. I think she noticed I'm just... not functioning at my usual level right now. 

I hate feeling like I'm letting people down, especially my clients. It’s just been so hard to push through this flatness. I hope it doesn't sound like I'm just making excuses? I really am trying my best to keep everything together.
Do you feel that this 'flat' feeling and the difficulty you are having with your work are causing you a significant amount of distress or emotional pain?

Um... emotional pain? No, no, I wouldn't call it that. I mean, I don't want to sound dramatic or anything. 

It's just... well, it's a little frustrating, I guess? But I'm not, like, sitting around crying or feeling completely devastated. I just feel bad that I'm not pulling my weight at work the way I usually do. I really pride myself on being reliable, you know? So it's more just... disappointing to myself that I can't seem to snap out of it right now. 

But I wouldn't say it's causing me severe distress. I'm still functioning, mostly! I just need to figure out how to get back on track. Does that make sense? I hope I'm not coming across as someone who can't handle their responsibilities.
Do you feel that the level of difficulty you are having at work is much more severe than what would be expected given the situation with your relative moving in?

Um... I don't know if I'd say *much* more severe, but... well, like I mentioned a minute ago about missing those grant deadlines and my supervisor having to step in with my more demanding clients... I guess maybe it is a bit more than just normal stress? 

I mean, I'm still showing up to the office every single day, I promise I'm really trying. But as a social worker, I really feel like I should be better equipped to handle a family transition like this without it spilling over into my caseload. It's just... I usually handle stress so much better than this. I suppose the fact that I'm not functioning at my usual level is a sign that it's hitting me harder than I'd like to admit. 

I just feel so embarrassed that I'm not managing it perfectly. Do you think it's understandable that I'm struggling a little bit with the adjustment, or should I be handling it better by now?
When you feel this 'flatness' or disappointment in yourself, do you also find yourself feeling nervous, on edge, or worried about the future?

Um, nervous? Oh, no, I wouldn't say I'm nervous or... or on edge. I mean, I try to stay positive about the future, really I do! 

I guess I worry a tiny bit, just about making sure I'm doing a good job for my clients and being there for my family. But it's not like a constant, overwhelming panic or anything like that. I'm definitely not sitting around wringing my hands all day. It's just normal concern, I think? Like anyone would have when they're juggling a lot. 

I hope that's an okay answer? I just don't want you to think I'm falling apart or, you know, constantly anxious. I'm really trying to keep a good perspective on things.
Aside from the feeling of being 'flat' or disconnected, have you found yourself feeling significantly sad or prone to crying since your relative moved in?

Oh, goodness, no. I haven't been... I'm definitely not crying or feeling terribly sad. 

I mean, I really try to keep a brave face, especially for my family and my clients. It's really just that... that flat feeling we talked about. I promise I'm not sitting around weeping or feeling completely miserable. I try to stay as upbeat as I can, all things considered. I know how important it is to keep a positive attitude, so I really make an effort to do that.

I think I'm doing an okay job of holding it together emotionally... at least, I hope I am? Does that sound like a healthy response to you? I just really don't want you to think I'm completely falling apart over here.
Have you noticed any physical tension in your body, like muscle tightness or an inability to relax, since your relative moved in?

Physical tension? Oh, um, no, I don't think so. I mean, maybe my shoulders get a tiny bit stiff sometimes, but I'm pretty sure that's just from hunching over my desk doing case notes all day. 

It's definitely not an inability to relax or anything like that. I always make a point to try and unwind in the evenings. I know how important self-care is, especially in social work, so I really do my best to practice what I preach to my clients. I'm definitely not walking around all clenched up or stressed out physically, I promise. 

Is it normal to just have a little bit of regular muscle stiffness from working, though? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture and that I'm handling the physical side of things okay.
Aside from the trouble with your work deadlines, have you noticed yourself acting differently in your relationships or your daily routines in a way that feels out of character for you?

Um, acting differently? Well, I wouldn't say out of character, exactly. I mean, I'm still me, just trying to keep everything running smoothly for everyone. 

There is... well, I guess there's one tiny thing, but I'm sure it's just a silly stress quirk. I've noticed, just a few times in team meetings, or... um, occasionally with clients, I've caught myself arranging my pens in these exact little patterns on the desk. Or sometimes I'll accidentally repeat a phrase someone just said right out loud before I can stop myself. 

It's really nothing major, I promise! It's just that sometimes people will give me a funny look, kind of like I’ve stepped outside the room somehow, you know? But I'm sure everyone has little nervous habits when they're juggling a lot, right? I'm trying really hard to be more mindful of it so I don't come across as unprofessional to my colleagues or the people I'm helping. That's just a normal response to having a lot on my plate, don't you think? I really hope it doesn't make me sound too strange.

When you arrange your pens or repeat those phrases, do you feel an internal pressure or a sense of 'must' do it to prevent something bad from happening, or is it more like an automatic habit you just find yourself doing?

Oh, no, definitely nothing like that. There's no... I don't feel like something terrible will happen if I don't do it. I promise it's not that. It’s really just an automatic habit. I just sort of realize I'm doing it after the fact, almost like I just zoned out for a second and my hands or my mouth just kept going. 

I know what you mean, though, like a compulsion, right? With my background in social work, I feel like I'd definitely recognize if it was getting into that sort of territory. It's really just a mindless little thing I do without thinking. I definitely don't believe that arranging my pens is keeping the world spinning or anything like that. 

It's really just like someone tapping their foot or biting their nails when they're distracted. That's a pretty standard, normal response to being overwhelmed, isn't it? Just an automatic fidget? I just want to reassure you that I'm not having any extreme thoughts about it or anything. I'm keeping a really good perspective on things, I really am. That makes sense, doesn't it?

Have you noticed any other changes in your behavior, such as acting out, becoming more irritable, or perhaps withdrawing from your friends or family more than you usually would since this all started?

Irritable? Oh, no, I don't think I've been irritable or acting out. I try really hard to maintain a positive attitude and be pleasant with everyone, especially my family and clients. I'm definitely not the type to snap at people or cause any kind of scene. 

But, um... withdrawing? Well, I wouldn't call it withdrawing exactly. It's more like... I'm just focusing on my responsibilities right now. I guess, if I'm being completely honest—and I really want to be helpful here—what finally made me realize I should talk to someone is that... well, I feel like the part of me that used to really reach out for people and, you know, take joy in my work and my hobbies... it's just gone very quiet lately. 

I used to love going to yoga, visiting art galleries, even just journaling in the evenings, but lately, I'm mostly just moving through my obligations. Like I'm just going through the motions to make sure everyone else is taken care of. 

I know it sounds a little bit flat, but I'm sure it's just burnout, right? I mean, in my field, compassion fatigue is so common, and I'm probably just needing a little reset. I'm still getting everything done, I promise. It's perfectly normal to just feel a little less enthusiastic when you're carrying a heavy load, don't you think? I just want to make sure I'm not making a bigger deal out of it than I should be.
Since your relative moved in, have you felt physically restless, such as an inability to sit still or a constant need to be moving?

Physically restless? Oh, no, I haven't noticed anything like that. I mean, even with the transition of my relative moving in—which, you know, takes a little adjusting for everyone—I'm definitely not pacing the floors or anything like that. 

I actually spend quite a bit of time just sitting quietly. I wouldn't want to be disruptive by constantly moving around the house, anyway. I try really hard to be considerate of the shared space and keep things peaceful for us both. 

So, no, I don't have that inability to sit still at all. I'm actually very good at staying seated and just... keeping calm physically. That's a good sign, isn't it? That I'm managing the household changes well enough to not be bouncing off the walls?
When you think about this 'flat' feeling and the fact that you aren't performing at your usual level, do you find yourself feeling a sense of personal failure or hopelessness about your situation?

Oh, gosh, no. No, I definitely don't feel hopeless. I mean... I know I mentioned feeling a bit flat, but I haven't given up or anything like that. I certainly don't see it as a personal failure. In my line of work, we talk so much about giving ourselves grace during tough times, and I... I really try to practice what I preach. 

I'm just viewing it as a temporary lull, you know? I'm keeping a very optimistic outlook, I promise. I know how concerning it can be when someone slips into that kind of despair, so I make absolutely sure to stay positive. I'm still showing up and doing my best every single day. That's the right way to handle it, isn't it? As long as I'm not losing hope and I'm keeping a good attitude, I'm doing okay, right?
Do you find yourself feeling any recurring, persistent, or intrusive thoughts that you have a hard time stopping, even when you try to focus on other things?

Intrusive thoughts? Oh, um... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I certainly don't have anything persistent or... or anything I can't stop. 

I know sometimes people get those awful, repetitive thoughts that just take over, but I'm very careful not to let my mind go there. As a social worker, I'm pretty well-versed in grounding techniques and mindfulness, so if my mind ever starts to wander or if I feel a little overwhelmed by my to-do list, I just redirect my focus. I'm actually quite good at keeping my thoughts organized and productive. 

I try to keep my mind on positive things, like how I can best support my clients and my family. So, no, nothing intrusive or hard to stop. I'm keeping a very good handle on my thoughts, I assure you. That's exactly what I should be doing, right? Just staying focused and not letting my mind run away with things?

While you mentioned you don't feel nervous or on edge, have you noticed any physical signs of anxiety, such as a racing heart, shallow breathing, or a sense of unease in your stomach when you are at home with your relative?

Physical signs? Oh, no, definitely not. I haven't noticed my heart racing or any kind of stomach ache at all. I mean, I know it's totally normal for people to carry tension in their bodies when there are changes at home, but I'm really careful not to let that happen. 

I actually make it a point to practice deep, diaphragmatic breathing—just as a healthy habit, you know, given my line of work. So my breathing is definitely not shallow. I feel like it's so important to model a calm physical presence, especially when you're sharing a space with a relative. I wouldn't want them to pick up on any nervous energy from me and feel like they're a burden. 

So, physically, I feel completely fine and settled. That's a good way to handle the transition, isn't it? Just making sure I keep my body relaxed so the whole house stays peaceful?
Even though you mentioned you don't feel hopeless or sad, have you noticed yourself feeling 'down,' 'blue,' or just generally unhappy since your relative moved in?

Oh, no, I wouldn't say 'blue' or unhappy at all. I mean, I know it's a big adjustment having family move in, and sometimes people get a little down when their routines change, but I really haven't felt that way. 

I actually think it's been a wonderful opportunity to practice patience and gratitude. I try to wake up every morning and just focus on the positives of having them here. As a social worker, I'm always telling my clients how important it is to reframe situations, so I've been very diligent about doing that myself. 

I might feel a little... tired at the end of the day, just from the extra responsibilities, but certainly not unhappy or down. I'm keeping my spirits up, I really am. I think it's so important to keep the home environment cheerful, don't you? It's better for everyone if I just stay upbeat and positive about the whole thing, right?

Even though you don't feel 'blue,' have you noticed that you have lost the ability to feel pleasure or enjoyment in things you used to love, like your yoga or art galleries, compared to how you felt before your relative moved in?

Well, um... I wouldn't say I've completely lost the ability to enjoy things. That sounds so... so severe, you know? I still think yoga is wonderful, and art galleries are lovely. I really do. 

But... I suppose... if I'm being completely honest, and I want to make sure I'm giving you the right information... it's just that lately, I've noticed things feel a little different. I guess that's actually what finally made me decide to come in and talk to someone. It’s just... the part of me that used to really reach out for people, or get that spark of joy from my work, or going to yoga, or walking through a gallery... even just sitting quietly and journaling... it’s all gone very, very quiet. 

I don't think it's a bad thing, necessarily! I’m still doing everything I need to do. I’m just mostly moving through my obligations right now, making sure everyone else is taken care of. That makes sense, doesn't it? When you have a lot on your plate, it's normal for those extra little joys to take a backseat while you focus on being responsible? I'm just trying to be responsible.

You mentioned that your supervisor had to move some of your more demanding clients to other clinicians because you were not functioning at your usual level; would you say this difficulty in meeting your professional responsibilities is causing you significant distress or impairment in your daily life?

Well, um... "significant distress" sounds a bit, you know, heavy. I wouldn't want to overstate it or make it sound worse than it is. I mean, I am still showing up to work every single day! I make sure I'm there, and I really try to put on a brave face for everyone. 

But... I suppose if I'm being completely transparent... yes, I’m just not functioning at my usual level right now. I actually, um... I missed a few grant deadlines recently, which is really embarrassing for me to admit. And, like you mentioned, my supervisor has quietly moved some of my more demanding clients to other clinicians. 

I don't want it to seem like I'm falling apart, though. I try to look at it as my supervisor just being supportive, you know? Giving me a little grace and a lighter caseload while I adjust to everything. It stings a little because I pride myself on my work, but I'm still managing the clients I have left. It’s okay to accept a little help and step back just a bit when things are a lot, right? I’m still being a good professional by letting my team support me, don't you think?
